And.documentation: Returns true only when both boolean operands evaluate to true.

operands.name: left
operands.documentation: A boolean expression. A comparison that produced NULL counts as unknown here, not as false.

operands.name: right
operands.documentation: A boolean expression, evaluated under the same rules.

examples.sql: SELECT name FROM $planets WHERE gravity > 5 AND number_of_moons = 0;
SELECT FALSE AND NULL, TRUE AND NULL;

And.notes: AND is three-valued. FALSE wins over an unknown - `FALSE AND NULL` is FALSE, because no value of the unknown side could make the pair true - while `TRUE AND NULL` is NULL. Only a TRUE result passes a WHERE clause, so a row whose condition is NULL is dropped exactly as a false one is.

ArrayContainsAll.documentation: Returns true when the left array contains all values from the right array.

operands.name: array
operands.documentation: The array to search.

operands.name: values
operands.documentation: The array of values that must ALL be present for the result to be true.

Arrow.documentation: Returns the selected JSON value from a document or JSON-like value.

operands.name: document
operands.documentation: The JSON document to read from.

operands.name: path
operands.documentation: The key or path to select. A bare key (`'city'`), a JSONPath (`'$.contact.email'`) and an RFC 6901 pointer (`'/contact/email'`) all name the same thing. A path that is not present gives NULL, not an error.

Arrow.notes: `->` keeps the value as JSON, so a selected string arrives still quoted (`"Earth"`); `->>` is the form that gives the text itself (`Earth`). That is the difference between the two, and the usual cause of a comparison against a string literal not matching. The result type is dynamic because the selected JSON value may be scalar, object, array, or null.

AtArrow.documentation: Returns true when the left array contains any of the values provided by the right array.

operands.name: array
operands.documentation: The array to search.

operands.name: values
operands.documentation: The array of values to look for. ANY one of them being present is enough; an empty array on this side matches nothing.

AtArrow.notes: `@>` is ANY, `@>>` is ALL - the pair is easy to mix up. `['a','b'] @> ['a','z']` is TRUE because one value matched; the same operands under `@>>` are FALSE.

AtQuestion.documentation: Returns true when the supplied JSON path expression matches within the left document.

operands.name: document
operands.documentation: The JSON document to test.

operands.name: path
operands.documentation: The path to look for. It is resolved to RFC 6901 tokens once, when the query is planned.

AtQuestion.notes: The path must be a literal — it is resolved to RFC 6901 tokens once when the query is planned, using the same resolver `->` uses, so `doc @? 'city'`, `doc @? '$.contact.email'` and `doc @? '/contact/email'` all name the same thing. Existence is not extraction: a path whose value is JSON `null` is TRUE here, while `doc->'key' IS NOT NULL` is FALSE. A NULL document row is NULL; a row whose bytes are not valid JSON is an error, never a silent false.

BitwiseAnd.documentation: Combines integer operands using a bitwise AND operation.

operands.name: left
operands.documentation: An integer value.

operands.name: right
operands.documentation: An integer value. The result keeps the operands' integer width rather than widening to 64-bit.

BitwiseOr.documentation: Combines integer operands using a bitwise OR operation.

operands.name: left
operands.documentation: An integer value.

operands.name: right
operands.documentation: An integer value. The result keeps the operands' integer width rather than widening to 64-bit.

BitwiseXor.documentation: Combines integer operands using a bitwise exclusive OR operation.

operands.name: left
operands.documentation: An integer value.

operands.name: right
operands.documentation: An integer value.

BitwiseXor.notes: `^` is exclusive OR, not exponentiation - a habit worth checking when porting SQL from systems where it raises to a power.

Divide.documentation: Returns the quotient of two numeric operands.

operands.name: dividend
operands.documentation: The value to divide. Two integers still divide to a FLOAT - use `DIV` for integer division.

operands.name: divisor
operands.documentation: The value to divide by. Dividing by zero yields infinity rather than raising, because the result is floating point.

Divide.notes: `/` is true division: `5 / 2` is 2.5, never 2. A DECIMAL operand keeps the result DECIMAL; every other combination gives FLOAT, and `1 / 0` is therefore `inf` rather than an error.

Eq.documentation: Returns true when both operands compare equal.

operands.name: left
operands.documentation: The value to compare. Numeric types compare across the family, so `1 = 1.0` is true.

operands.name: right
operands.documentation: The value to compare it against. It must be type-compatible with the left - a number and a string are rejected rather than coerced.

Eq.notes: Comparison is three-valued: NULL on either side gives NULL, never true or false, and `NULL = NULL` is NULL too - `IS NULL` is the test for absence. String comparison is case-sensitive (`'Mars' = 'mars'` is false), unlike column NAMES, which are not.

Gt.documentation: Returns true when the left operand is greater than the right operand.

operands.name: left
operands.documentation: The value to compare. Strings order byte-by-byte, so uppercase sorts before lowercase.

operands.name: right
operands.documentation: The value to compare it against.

Gt.notes: NULL on either side gives NULL, so ordering comparisons never match an absent value.

GtEq.documentation: Returns true when the left operand is greater than or equal to the right operand.

operands.name: left
operands.documentation: The value to compare.

operands.name: right
operands.documentation: The value to compare it against.

GtEq.notes: NULL on either side gives NULL, so ordering comparisons never match an absent value.

ILike.documentation: Returns true when the left string matches the SQL ILIKE pattern on the right without case sensitivity.

operands.name: haystack
operands.documentation: The value tested against the pattern.

operands.name: pattern
operands.documentation: A SQL LIKE pattern, matched without regard to case: `%` matches any run of characters, `_` matches exactly one.

examples.sql: SELECT name FROM $planets WHERE name ILIKE 'ma%';

ILike.notes: Case folding is ASCII-only: `'ABC' ILIKE 'abc'` is true, but `'ÉCOLE' ILIKE 'école'` is FALSE - accented and other non-ASCII letters are compared as written. Where that matters, fold explicitly with a function instead.

IPContainedBy.documentation: Returns true when the left IPv4 address falls inside the network given on the right in CIDR notation, for example `ip <<= '10.0.0.0/8'`. Comparison is on the underlying 32-bit address, so it is a single mask-and-compare per row with no text parsing.

operands.name: address
operands.documentation: An IPv4 address. It is held as its 32-bit integer value, which is why the signature below reads INTEGER.

operands.name: network
operands.documentation: The network to test against, in CIDR notation. The prefix length is required: an address without one is rejected.

IPContainedBy.notes: Spelling follows PostgreSQL, CockroachDB and DuckDB's inet extension. A NULL address is not contained by any network and yields false. An invalid or prefix-less CIDR raises rather than matching nothing.

IPContains.documentation: Returns true when the network on the left, in CIDR notation, contains the IPv4 address on the right, for example `'10.0.0.0/8' >>= ip`. The mirror of `<<=`.

operands.name: network
operands.documentation: The network to test against, in CIDR notation, with its prefix length.

operands.name: address
operands.documentation: An IPv4 address. It is held as its 32-bit integer value, which is why the signature below reads INTEGER.

IPContains.notes: Spelling follows PostgreSQL, CockroachDB and DuckDB's inet extension.

InList.documentation: Returns true when the left operand matches any element in the right-hand list or array.

operands.name: value
operands.documentation: The value to look for.

operands.name: list
operands.documentation: The values to look in - a parenthesised list, or an array-valued expression. Every element must share one type; a mixed list, NULL included, is rejected at plan time rather than being silently skipped.

examples.sql: SELECT name FROM $planets WHERE name IN ('Earth', 'Mars');

InList.notes: IN is a shorthand for a chain of `=`, and inherits its rules: the comparison is exact and case-sensitive. A list mixing types - `IN (NULL, 2)` among them - is an error, not a match against the elements that do share a type.

Like.documentation: Returns true when the left string matches the SQL LIKE pattern on the right.

operands.name: haystack
operands.documentation: The value tested against the pattern. VARBINARY is accepted as well as text, and is matched as bytes.

operands.name: pattern
operands.documentation: A SQL LIKE pattern: `%` matches any run of characters including none, `_` matches exactly one, and every other character matches itself. The whole value must match, not part of it - `'abcd' LIKE 'a_c'` is false. A column is accepted here, not only a literal; a literal is what lets the planner fuse the match into the scan.

examples.sql: SELECT name FROM $planets WHERE name LIKE 'Ma%';

Like.notes: Matching is case-sensitive; ILIKE is the case-insensitive form. A NULL on either side is not matched.

LongArrow.documentation: Returns the selected JSON value as text (nvarchar), from a document given as text or binary JSON.

operands.name: document
operands.documentation: The JSON document to read from.

operands.name: path
operands.documentation: The key or path to select, in the same spellings `->` accepts. A path that is not present gives NULL.

LongArrow.notes: Use `->>` when the value is going to be compared with a string literal: `->` would leave it JSON-quoted and the comparison would not match.

Lt.documentation: Returns true when the left operand is less than the right operand.

operands.name: left
operands.documentation: The value to compare. Strings order byte-by-byte, so uppercase sorts before lowercase.

operands.name: right
operands.documentation: The value to compare it against.

Lt.notes: NULL on either side gives NULL, so ordering comparisons never match an absent value.

LtEq.documentation: Returns true when the left operand is less than or equal to the right operand.

operands.name: left
operands.documentation: The value to compare.

operands.name: right
operands.documentation: The value to compare it against.

LtEq.notes: NULL on either side gives NULL, so ordering comparisons never match an absent value.

MapAccess.documentation: Returns the element at the requested index from an array, string, or blob-like value.

operands.name: value
operands.documentation: The array, string or blob to read from.

operands.name: index
operands.documentation: The zero-based position to read: 0 is the first element. A negative index counts back from the end, so -1 is the last. An index past either end gives NULL rather than raising.

MapAccess.notes: Subscript access is ZERO-based and accepts negative indexes, which count back from the end: `[0]` is the first element and `[-1]` the last. Most SQL dialects index arrays from 1, so a query ported from one of those reads the WRONG element rather than erroring - an out-of-range index gives NULL, so nothing signals the mistake. For arrays the result type depends on the array element type, so the exported result type may be dynamic.

Minus.documentation: Returns the difference between two numeric, date, timestamp, or interval-compatible operands.

operands.name: left
operands.documentation: The value to subtract from.

operands.name: right
operands.documentation: The value to subtract. Subtracting one TIMESTAMP from another gives an INTERVAL; subtracting an INTERVAL from a timestamp gives a timestamp.

examples.sql: SELECT name, aphelion - perihelion FROM $planets LIMIT 3;
SELECT CAST('2026-03-01' AS TIMESTAMP) - INTERVAL '1' MONTH;

Minus.notes: Unlike addition, subtraction is not symmetric across types: a timestamp minus an interval is a timestamp, but an interval minus a timestamp is not accepted.

Modulo.documentation: Returns the remainder after division of the left numeric operand by the right numeric operand.

operands.name: dividend
operands.documentation: The value to divide. Its sign is the sign of the result.

operands.name: divisor
operands.documentation: The value to divide by.

Modulo.notes: The remainder takes the sign of the DIVIDEND, not the divisor: `-7 % 2` is -1 and `7 % -2` is 1. That is C and Go's rule, not Python's, where `-7 % 2` is 1.

Multiply.documentation: Returns the product of two numeric operands.

operands.name: left
operands.documentation: A numeric value.

operands.name: right
operands.documentation: A numeric value. The result takes the wider of the two types - see Signatures.

MyIntegerDivide.documentation: Divides two integers and truncates the result toward zero.

operands.name: dividend
operands.documentation: The integer to divide.

operands.name: divisor
operands.documentation: The integer to divide by.

MyIntegerDivide.notes: Truncation is toward zero, not toward minus infinity: `-7 DIV 2` is -3, where a floor division would give -4.

NotEq.documentation: Returns true when the operands do not compare equal.

operands.name: left
operands.documentation: The value to compare.

operands.name: right
operands.documentation: The value to compare it against. It must be type-compatible with the left.

examples.sql: SELECT name FROM $planets WHERE name != 'Earth' LIMIT 3;

NotEq.notes: `!=` does not mean "everything else": a row whose value is NULL answers NULL, not true, so it is dropped by the WHERE clause. Of the nine planets one has a surface pressure of 0 and four have none recorded, so `surface_pressure != 0` returns four rows, not eight - `OR surface_pressure IS NULL` is how the unknown rows are kept.

NotILike.documentation: Returns true when the left string does not match the SQL ILIKE pattern on the right.

operands.name: haystack
operands.documentation: The value tested against the pattern.

operands.name: pattern
operands.documentation: A SQL LIKE pattern, matched without regard to ASCII case.

examples.sql: SELECT name FROM $planets WHERE name NOT ILIKE 'ma%' LIMIT 3;

NotILike.notes: Case folding is ASCII-only, exactly as for ILIKE.

NotInList.documentation: Returns true when the left operand does not match any element in the right-hand list or array.

operands.name: value
operands.documentation: The value to look for.

operands.name: list
operands.documentation: The values to look in. Every element must share one type; a mixed list is rejected at plan time.

examples.sql: SELECT name FROM $planets WHERE name NOT IN ('Earth', 'Mars') LIMIT 3;

NotInList.notes: Like `!=`, a row whose value is NULL answers NULL rather than true, so it does not survive a WHERE clause.

NotLike.documentation: Returns true when the left string does not match the SQL LIKE pattern on the right.

operands.name: haystack
operands.documentation: The value tested against the pattern.

operands.name: pattern
operands.documentation: A SQL LIKE pattern: `%` matches any run of characters, `_` matches exactly one. The whole value must match for the row to be excluded.

examples.sql: SELECT name FROM $planets WHERE name NOT LIKE 'Ma%' LIMIT 3;

NotLike.notes: Case-sensitive, like `LIKE` itself. NOT ILIKE is the case-insensitive form.

NotRLike.documentation: Returns true when the left string does not match the regular expression on the right.

operands.name: haystack
operands.documentation: The value tested against the expression.

operands.name: regex
operands.documentation: The regular expression that must not match. It matches anywhere in the value unless anchored.

examples.sql: SELECT name FROM $planets WHERE name NOT RLIKE '^M' LIMIT 3;

Or.documentation: Returns true when either boolean operand evaluates to true.

operands.name: left
operands.documentation: A boolean expression. A comparison that produced NULL counts as unknown here, not as false.

operands.name: right
operands.documentation: A boolean expression, evaluated under the same rules.

examples.sql: SELECT name FROM $planets WHERE name = 'Earth' OR name = 'Mars';
SELECT TRUE OR NULL, FALSE OR NULL;

Or.notes: OR is three-valued, and the mirror of AND: TRUE wins over an unknown - `TRUE OR NULL` is TRUE - while `FALSE OR NULL` is NULL, not FALSE.

Plus.documentation: Returns the sum of two numeric or interval-compatible operands.

operands.name: left
operands.documentation: The value to add to. A DATE or TIMESTAMP is accepted only with an INTERVAL on the other side - two dates cannot be added.

operands.name: right
operands.documentation: The value to add. Mixing numeric types widens the result: INTEGER with FLOAT gives FLOAT, INTEGER with DECIMAL gives DECIMAL.

examples.sql: SELECT CAST('2026-01-01' AS DATE) + INTERVAL '1' MONTH;

Plus.notes: Adding NULL gives NULL. Date arithmetic is only ever date-plus-interval, and the result is a TIMESTAMP even when the operand was a DATE - see Signatures.

RLike.documentation: Returns true when the left string matches the regular expression on the right.

operands.name: haystack
operands.documentation: The value tested against the expression.

operands.name: regex
operands.documentation: The regular expression to match. Unlike LIKE, it matches anywhere in the value unless anchored with `^` and `$`.

examples.sql: SELECT name FROM $planets WHERE name RLIKE '^M.*s$';

RLike.notes: A regular expression is more expressive than a LIKE pattern and more expensive to run; prefer LIKE when a prefix or suffix match is all that is needed.

ShiftLeft.documentation: Shifts the bits of the left integer operand left by the number of positions in the right operand.

operands.name: value
operands.documentation: The integer whose bits are shifted.

operands.name: count
operands.documentation: How many positions to shift by, 0..63.

ShiftLeft.notes: The shift count must be 0..63 - the operands are 64-bit integers, and a count outside that range fails loud ('bitwise_shl: shift count out of range') rather than wrapping or saturating.

ShiftRight.documentation: Shifts the bits of the left integer operand right by the number of positions in the right operand.

operands.name: value
operands.documentation: The integer whose bits are shifted. The shift is arithmetic, so the sign is preserved.

operands.name: count
operands.documentation: How many positions to shift by, 0..63.

ShiftRight.notes: Right shift is ARITHMETIC, not logical: the sign bit is copied, so `-1 >> 1` is -1 and a negative value never becomes positive by shifting. The shift count must be 0..63 - the operands are 64-bit integers, and a count outside that range fails loud ('bitwise_shr: shift count out of range') rather than wrapping or saturating.

StringConcat.documentation: Concatenates the left and right string or blob operands.

operands.name: left
operands.documentation: The value to concatenate to.

operands.name: right
operands.documentation: The value to append. It must be the SAME string type as the left - VARCHAR with VARCHAR, VARBINARY with VARBINARY - and a number must be cast first.

StringConcat.notes: The operands must be the same string type; mixing VARCHAR and VARBINARY is rejected rather than silently coerced. `x || NULL` is NULL for every row - it is not treated as an empty string - but the expression still carries the string operand's type.

Xor.documentation: Returns true when exactly one boolean operand evaluates to true.

operands.name: left
operands.documentation: A boolean expression.

operands.name: right
operands.documentation: A boolean expression.

Xor.notes: Unlike AND and OR, XOR has no dominant value: the answer always depends on both sides, so NULL on either side gives NULL.
